findings.claim: The model answer says the reform's recognition of unfortified wines 'legitimised the vino de pasto movement'. It also says vintage-dated wines may 'now' be labelled, and the accept list takes 'vino de pasto was legalised'.
findings.finalFix: ans: 'It reopened the region to its own history. The ageing zone had been confined to Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar (the famous triangle) and was extended across the wider production zone, so towns like Trebujena, Chipiona, Chiclana and Rota that had always grown grapes may now age wine under the DO. Fortification stopped being compulsory for wines that reach the minimum strength for their style naturally (then 15% for fino and manzanilla and 17% for oloroso; a 2025 amendment lowered fino, manzanilla and pale cream to 14%). The low-alcohol vino de pasto whites remain outside the DO and are being pursued as a separate DO, Vino de Albariza. Named pagos, the traditional delimited vineyard districts, may now appear on labels. And historic varieties beyond Palomino, Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel (Beba, Perruno, Vejeriego, Cañocazo and the two Mantúos) were restored to the permitted list.
